title: Greedy vs Dynamic Programming — Telling Them Apart
summary: How to tell, before you start coding, whether a problem needs greedy's single pass or DP's full search over choices — the decision this entire group has been building toward.

slides.markdown:
Greedy and DP both optimize over a sequence of choices, and both need optimal substructure. The difference is what happens **after** a choice is made: greedy locks it in forever; DP keeps every option alive and combines the best of each.

This topic is the payoff of everything else in this group — `greedy-fundamentals` showed a greedy strategy can look right and be wrong; `exchange-argument` gave you the proof technique; the intervening problems gave you worked examples. Here, that all becomes a decision procedure you can run *before* writing code, so you're choosing the right tool on purpose rather than discovering the mismatch after debugging a wrong answer.

slides.subTitle: Can a local choice be revisited later?
slides.markdown:
Ask this concretely: if I make the locally best choice right now, could a **different** choice at this same step ever turn out to have been better, once I see more of the problem? If genuinely no — the locally best choice is always safe — greedy applies. If yes, or if you can't rule it out, DP's full exploration is what you need.

This single question is the compressed form of the greedy-choice property from `greedy-fundamentals`. The rest of this topic gives you faster, more concrete versions of the same question to apply under time pressure, since "could this ever be revisited" is sometimes hard to answer in the abstract but easy to answer once you look at the problem's specific structure.

slides.sectionTitle: Fractional vs. 0/1 knapsack, side by side
slides.markdown:
The clearest illustration in this whole curriculum: identical problem statement, one word changed, and the correct technique flips entirely.

![Fractional knapsack greedily slicing a divisible item, versus 0/1 knapsack where whole items and a 2D DP table are required](assets/greedy-vs-dp-knapsack.svg)

Divisibility is the entire hinge: fractional allows topping off with a slice of the next-best item, so no earlier choice ever forecloses a better outcome — greedy applies. 0/1 forbids that, so an early choice genuinely can foreclose a better combination — DP is required.

assets.alt: Fractional knapsack greedily slicing a divisible item, versus 0/1 knapsack where whole items and a 2D DP table are required

slides.sectionTitle: Reusing the ratio trick where it doesn't apply
slides.markdown:
Applying fractional knapsack's "sort by value/weight ratio, take greedily" directly to 0/1 knapsack is a specific, common version of the general mistake this group has been warning about. It produces a plausible-looking answer, often correct on small hand-picked examples, and wrong once an example is constructed where the best-ratio item's weight doesn't divide capacity cleanly.

Concrete counterexample: capacity 10, items (weight 6, value 30) and (weight 5, value 24) and (weight 5, value 24). Best ratio is the first item (5/weight), greedily taking it uses 6 of 10 capacity for value 30, leaving 4 capacity — not enough for either remaining item. The optimal 0/1 answer skips the best-ratio item entirely and takes both weight-5 items for value 48. Ratio-greedy never even considers this.

| Points toward greedy | Points toward DP |
|---|---|
| A single sortable criterion decides every choice | Multiple criteria interact (weight AND value, position AND count-used) |
| A choice, once made, is never reconsidered by the rest of the algorithm | The best choice at a step depends on choices made elsewhere |
| You can sketch an exchange argument without hitting a counterexample | Every attempted exchange argument produces a counterexample |
| Divisible / infinitely reusable resources | All-or-nothing / limited-count resources |

No single row is decisive alone — use this as a fast first hypothesis, then actually try to prove or break it (the discipline from `greedy-fundamentals` and `exchange-argument`) rather than trusting the checklist as a final verdict.

slides.sectionTitle: Greedy as a special case of DP
slides.markdown:
Every greedy algorithm can be viewed as a DP recurrence that happens to **collapse**: instead of trying every choice and taking the best (`dp[i] = best over all valid choices`), the recurrence's own structure guarantees one specific choice is always the best, so the "try every choice" search degenerates into "always pick this one."

This reframing is useful for a specific reason: it tells you that reaching for the full DP recurrence first, then noticing it always resolves to the same choice, is itself a valid way to *discover* that a problem is greedy — you don't need to spot the greedy shortcut immediately. If you write out the DP and the `max`/`min` over choices always lands on the same option regardless of the other state, that's your proof the collapse is legitimate.

slides.sectionTitle: Trusting a greedy that only passed given examples
slides.markdown:
The single riskiest moment in this whole comparison: a greedy idea passes the interviewer's example, feels intuitive, and gets shipped as the answer without the correctness check. Small given examples are chosen for clarity, not for adversarial coverage — `greedy-fundamentals`' coin-change trap and this topic's knapsack counterexample both pass plenty of "reasonable" test cases before failing on a specifically constructed one.

The fix is the same discipline repeated throughout this group: after a greedy idea works on the given example, spend a moment actively trying to construct a case that breaks it, using the signal checklist to guess where the fragility might be (divisibility? multiple competing criteria?). If you can't break it after a genuine attempt, say so explicitly and sketch why, rather than presenting untested confidence as a finished proof.

In an interview, state the exchange argument's shape rather than just asserting correctness: "I'm sorting by X and taking greedily; this is safe because if an optimal solution didn't pick the greedy choice here, I can swap it in without losing anything, since [the specific reason]." Three sentences, and it's the difference between "I have a hunch" and "I have a proof sketch."

If you can't complete that sentence with a real reason — if the "since" clause is vague or you're not sure — that's itself useful information: it's a signal to either dig for the actual reason before committing, or to say plainly "I'm not fully certain this greedy is safe; let me check for a counterexample" and spend a minute doing exactly that, live, in front of the interviewer. Both responses read far better than confidently asserting an unproven greedy.

slides.sectionTitle: Worked case study: activity selection, revisited
slides.markdown:
Run the checklist against `activity-selection` and its weighted variant, side by side: unweighted activity selection has a single sortable criterion (finish time) and a provable exchange argument (`exchange-argument` walked through it in full) — greedy applies cleanly. The moment a per-activity **value** is introduced, a second criterion enters that interacts with the first (an overlapping high-value activity can beat several low-value non-overlapping ones) — the exchange argument breaks, and the checklist correctly predicts DP is now needed.

This is the cleanest paired example in the curriculum for seeing the checklist in action on the *same underlying problem* before and after the change that breaks greedy — worth replaying mentally whenever you're unsure which side of the line a new problem falls on.

slides.sectionTitle: A decision procedure for time pressure
slides.markdown:
Under real interview time constraints, run this in order: **(1)** Does a single sortable criterion decide every choice, with no second competing factor? **(2)** Can you sketch, in one or two sentences, why swapping the locally-best choice into any alternative solution can't hurt? **(3)** Have you tried, even briefly, to construct a case where it fails?

If all three go through cleanly, commit to greedy and state the proof sketch unprompted. If step 1 already fails (multiple interacting criteria) or step 3 turns up a real counterexample, pivot to DP immediately rather than trying to patch the greedy idea — patching a broken greedy rarely produces a correct one, it usually just produces a greedy that's wrong on a narrower set of inputs.

slides.sectionTitle: When both work, but greedy is strictly better
slides.markdown:
Not every greedy-vs-DP question is about correctness — sometimes DP would also give the right answer, just at a worse complexity, and the real skill is noticing greedy is available and strictly preferable. `jump-game`, earlier in this group, is the clean example: a DP formulation of Jump Game II is correct but O(n²), while the greedy frontier-tracking approach is O(n) and loses no information the DP was actually using.

When you've confirmed greedy is *correct* via the checklist above, it's still worth asking whether a DP alternative exists and, if so, explicitly naming that greedy is preferred here on efficiency grounds — that's a more complete and more senior answer than treating "is it greedy or DP" as a binary fork with only one right answer per problem.
